title: Fasteners & Threaded Joints
summary: ISO metric threads, property classes, torque-preload relationship, and joint design rules for bolted connections that actually stay tight.

sections.heading: Bolts: The Most Common Failure
sections.content:
Most bolted joints do not fail by the bolt **stretching** — they fail because the bolt was **never tight enough** and came loose, or because it was **overtightened** and cracked. A bolt is a spring that clamps two parts; the joint is only as good as the **preload** (tension) locked into it. Vibration loosens joints by removing preload through cyclic slip — the classic cause of "the bolt was found on the floor".

Designing a bolted joint means: pick the thread and property class, target a preload, choose the tightening method, and verify the joint stays tight in service.

sections.heading: ISO Metric Threads & Property Classes
sections.content:
An ISO metric thread is designated **M8 × 1.25** — major diameter 8 mm, pitch 1.25 mm. Key terms: **major diameter** (nominal, the crest), **pitch diameter** (theoretical contact cylinder), **minor diameter** (root), and **pitch P** (distance between crests). Course threads (M8 × 1.25) resist stripping better; fine threads (M8 × 1) resist loosening better and give finer adjustment.

**Property classes** encode strength for carbon/alloy steel bolts:

- **8.8** → tensile strength $S_{ut} = 800$ MPa, yield $S_y = 640$ MPa (0.8 × 800).
- **10.9** → $S_{ut} = 1000$ MPa, yield 900 MPa.
- **12.9** → 1200 MPa / 1080 MPa — for high-strength applications, brittle, hydrogen-embrittlement sensitive, typically hex-socket (Allen) heads.

Match the property class to the joint load — upgrading from 8.8 to 10.9 buys 25% more preload capacity but also requires better tightening control.

sections.heading: Torque–Preload Relationship
sections.content:
Tightening torque divides roughly 50% into thread friction, 40% into head/nut friction, and only **10% into useful preload**. The empirical relation:

$$T = K \cdot F \cdot d$$

with $K$ the nut factor: 0.20 for **zinc-plated, as-received** steel; 0.15 lubricated; 0.25–0.30 for dry/rough surfaces. The scatter of $K$ means torque control gives only ±25–30% preload accuracy — acceptable for most joints, not for critical ones.

Design target: preload to about **70–90% of proof load**:

$$F \approx 0.7 \, F_p = 0.7 \, A_s \, S_p$$

Example — M10 class 8.8 (stress area $A_s = 58.0$ mm², proof $S_p = 580$ MPa):

$$F_p = 580 \times 58 = 33.6 \text{ kN}, \qquad F = 0.7 \times 33.6 = 23.5 \text{ kN}$$
$$T = K \cdot F \cdot d = 0.20 \times 23,500 \times 0.010 = 47 \text{ N·m}$$

For critical joints use **angle-controlled tightening** (turn-to-yield) or hydraulic tensioners, which cut preload scatter to ±5–10%.

sections.heading: Joint Stiffness & the Load Triangle
sections.content:
Preloaded parts carry external load as a **reduction of clamping** first, before the bolt sees additional tension. The stiffer the clamped parts relative to the bolt, the smaller the bolt load amplitude under fluctuating external load — the load triangle: external load $F_e$ splits into $F_e \cdot k_b/(k_b + k_c)$ on the bolt and the rest on the joint.

Design rules that keep joints tight:

- **Clamp length ≥ 2–3× bolt diameter** — short clamps (thin flanges) are springy and loosen easily.
- Use **through-bolts with nuts** over tapped blind holes when possible; a tapped hole concentrates stress in the housing threads.
- Include **hardened washers** under the head and nut to spread load and prevent embedment relaxation.
- Watch **embedment**: soft materials (aluminium, composites) settle under preload — retighten or over-preload to compensate.
- Keep the joint **under compression** in service: the joint separates when external load exceeds preload plus the joint's share — separation is usually a design failure, not a bolt failure.

sections.heading: Anti-Loosening Methods
sections.content:
Choose the locking method by vibration severity and reusability:

| Method | Principle | Reusable | Vibration rating |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nyloc / prevailing torque | Nylon insert creates drag | Somewhat | Good |
| Serrated flange | Teeth bite into surface | Yes | Good |
| Thread adhesive (Loctite) | Wicking anaerobe fills thread | No (reapply) | Very good |
| Lock washers (split) | Spring action | Yes | **Poor** — often useless in practice |
| Castellated + cotter pin | Positive lock | Yes | Excellent |
| Prevailing-torque wedge | Elastic wedge at 60° offset | Yes | Excellent (Stover/Nord-Lock family) |

Split lock washers remain the most *commonly specified* and *least effective* solution in real vibration tests. For safety-critical joints, prefer positive locks (cotter pins, stake nuts) or wedge-action washers.

sections.heading: Materials, Washers & Galvanic Care
sections.content:
Fastener selection crosses into materials:

- **Stainless A2/A4** — corrosion-resistant but prone to **galling** (cold-weld seizure) when tightened; use lubricant on threads.
- **Zinc-plated carbon steel** — the everyday default; plating thickness affects the nut factor $K$, so recalibrate torque after changing finish.
- **Aluminium + steel contact** — galvanic corrosion at the interface; use coated bolts or isolating washers in moist or marine environments.

Washer roles: **plain** spreads load and protects the surface; **hardened** under hardened heads/nuts prevents Brinelling of soft flanges; **Belleville (disc) springs** maintain preload through thermal expansion and long-term settlement of springy joints. A Belleville stack under a bolt can convert a "loosening" joint into a stable one without any thread-locking device.

keyTakeaways: Torque is ~10% useful preload: T = K·F·d with K ≈ 0.20 for plated steel; target F ≈ 0.7·proof load.
Tighten by angle or hydraulic tension for critical joints — torque control scatters ±25–30%.
Keep clamp length ≥ 2–3× bolt diameter and keep the joint under compression in service.
Split lock washers are poor anti-loosening devices; use prevailing-torque, wedge-action, or positive locks.
